newsitem.title: CYPRUS: U.S. will work on Cyprus solution, says top aide.
newsitem.headline: U.S. will work on Cyprus solution, says top aide.

text.p: The United States will push forward with its initiative to help reunite the divided island of Cyprus after U.S. presidential elections in November, a senior aide to President Bill Clinton said on Thursday.

Adviser George Stephanopoulos, in a telephone message to a congress of overseas Greek Cypriots meeting in Nicosia, said Clinton was committed to redoubling efforts to assist work for a settlement on the island.

"Obviously with the Greek elections in just a few weeks and our own elections coming up I think it is difficult to expect something before the elections," said Stephanopoulos, speaking from the White House.
"Cyprus has to be on the top of the peacekeeping and peacemaking agenda... he (Clinton) is determined to push forward after the elections," he said.
The island has been virtually partitioned since 1974 when Turkish troops invaded the island in the wake of a short-lived coup engineered by the military regime ruling Greece.

Only Turkey recognises a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state set up in the north of the island in 1983, where some 30,000 mainland troops are stationed, and the protracted dispute remains a source of tension between Turkey and Greece, its neighbour and NATO partner.

Tension in Cyprus has risen considerably in the past month after the killings of two Greek Cypriots by security forces and civilians in the Turkish-occupied areas during demonstrations against the division of the island.
Stephanopoulos said the incidents showed the status quo on the island was unjust and unsustainable.

Madeleine Albright, Washington's ambassador to the United Nations, visited Cyprus in July on a fact finding mission. But a planned military dialogue between the commanders of the Greek Cypriot national guard and the Turkish army to look at technical ways of defusing tension along the ceasefire line dividing the island has yet to start.
